title: Graphical tools in base R
source: Code from "Statistical Analysis using RStudio", UP Mindanao SPARCS on dev.to (April 2025)
intro: Watch RStudio draw four kinds of chart. For each line, the coach selects it in graphical-tools.R and presses Run. It explains the result after the chart appears in the Plots pane.

steps.title: Plots: plot()
steps.explain: `plot()` drew one point at x = 5, y = 5. It chooses what to draw from the data you give it, and two single numbers make one point. Both axes are labelled 5 because `plot()` uses the code you passed in as the axis labels.

steps.title: Lines: type = "l"
steps.explain: `1:10` is the whole numbers 1 to 10. When you give `plot()` one vector, it puts the values on the y-axis and their positions on the x-axis, labelled Index. `type="l"` joins the points with a line instead of drawing circles. `plot()` always starts a new chart. To add a line to a chart that is already drawn, use `lines()`.

steps.title: Pie chart: pie()

runs.code: pie(slices) # Creating a pie chart with the values of vector slices

steps.explain: `c()` combined 50, 20 and 30 into a vector called `slices`, which now appears in the Environment pane. `pie()` sizes each slice by its share of the total, so 50 fills half the circle. The slices are labelled 1, 2 and 3 because the vector has no names.

steps.title: Bar graph: barplot()

runs.code: frequencies <- c(3, 6, 9) # Y - axis of the bar graph
label <- c("X", "Y", "Z") # X - axis of the bar graph

steps.explain: `frequencies` sets the bar heights: 3, 6 and 9. `names.arg = label` writes X, Y and Z under the bars. All the bars start from the same baseline, so their heights are easier to compare than pie slices.
